answer: The crash isn't caused by model_to_dot() — it happens inside create_vgg_like_model() itself, since Keras allocates and initializes every layer's weight tensors as soon as the layer is built (eager mode), before you ever visualize anything. Stock VGG16 is only ~140M params (~550MB), which shouldn't exhaust 8GB, so the more likely culprit is a bug in your custom 'VGG16-like' builder — commonly forgetting a pooling/GlobalAveragePooling2D step before Flatten, which produces a huge feature vector feeding a Dense(4096) layer with billions of parameters. Before building the full model, sanity-check the architecture: build layer-by-layer and print `layer.compute_output_shape(...)`, or call `model.summary()`/`model.count_params()` right after construction and abort if it's unreasonable. There's no supported way to get 'shallow' architecture info (names/shapes/param counts) without Keras materializing the weight variables — that's inherent to how layers build. Also note `set_memory_growth` only applies to GPU/pluggable devices, which is why it raises on CPU.

`self.ids.Canvas...` / `canvas.ids.rect` resolves to Widget.canvas (the actual kivy.graphics.Canvas instruction group every widget has), not a widget you named 'Canvas' — that object has no `.ids`, hence the AttributeError. kv `id:` entries are only registered in the `ids` dict of the rule they're declared in (here `<Canvas_Widget>`), so `rect` lives in that widget instance's own `self.ids.rect`, not in MainWidget's ids. To reach it from MainWidget, give the Canvas_Widget instance itself an id when you place it inside `<MainWidget>`'s kv:
```
Canvas_Widget:
    id: canvas_widget
```
then in Python: `self.ids.canvas_widget.ids.rect.size`. Also double-check that `<MainWidget>` actually instantiates a `Canvas_Widget:` somewhere (your posted kv only shows a Button under it), since without that the id can't exist at all.

pandas removed `DataFrame.append()` in pandas 2.0 (deprecated since 1.4) — check your version first; if ≥2.0 the method no longer exists. Separately, 'append() missing one required positional argument: other' means `a.append(...)` is being called as an unbound method with no self bound, which happens if `a` is actually the class `pd.DataFrame` rather than an instance (e.g. `a` never got assigned `pd.DataFrame()`). Either way, don't loop `.append` — build a list and concat once:
```python
rows = [data.iloc[[i]] for i in wanted_indices]
a = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
```
or per-row: `a = pd.concat([a, data.iloc[[i]]], ignore_index=True)`. `iloc[[i]]` (list) keeps it a DataFrame row instead of a Series, which concat handles more predictably than mixing Series/array rows.

Two bugs: (1) your SQL has one `?` placeholder but you pass two values (x, y) — `SET valori=?` can only bind one; (2) you never filter by `id`, so even fixed it would overwrite every row identically. Since x is id=1 and y is id=2, run two parameterized updates and commit:
```python
connect.execute("UPDATE Valori_Textbox SET valori=? WHERE id=?", (x.get(), 1))
connect.execute("UPDATE Valori_Textbox SET valori=? WHERE id=?", (y.get(), 2))
new_connection.commit()
```
Missing `commit()` is a separate likely reason changes 'don't update' even once the syntax is fixed — sqlite3 won't persist writes until you commit. For a generic N-row version, use `executemany("UPDATE ... SET valori=? WHERE id=?", [(x.get(),1),(y.get(),2)])`.

The comprehension evaluates its right-hand side against the *original, unmodified* `subsets` at every step — the name `subsets` is only rebound to the new list after the whole comprehension finishes, so every lookup during it sees the initial array, not any partial results from earlier in that same comprehension. In the explicit for-loop, `subsets[index] = ...` mutates the list in place immediately, so later iterations read values already changed by earlier ones — a partially-updated array, not the original. That's the whole discrepancy. If you want the loop's mutate-as-you-go behavior in a comprehension you can't get it directly (comprehensions snapshot the source); if you want the comprehension's 'always read original' behavior in the loop, read from a copy: `orig = subsets.copy()` and index `orig[...]` on the right-hand side inside the loop instead of `subsets[...]`.

`sympy.stats.E()` only expands linearity automatically when it can resolve a concrete distribution; with bare dependent symbols it either evaluates numerically or (incorrectly) collapses `E(X)` to `X`. What you want is the unevaluated `Expectation` object and its dedicated `.expand()` method, which applies linearity symbolically without needing any distribution:
```python
from sympy.stats import Expectation
from sympy import symbols
X, Y = symbols('X Y')
expr = Expectation(X + Expectation(X*Y) + 2*X - Y)
result = expr.expand()
print(result)  # 3*E(X) + E(X*Y) - E(Y)
```
`Expectation.expand()` distributes over sums, pulls out constants, and leaves `E(X*Y)` untouched since X and Y are dependent — exactly the output you want. Passing `evaluate=False` to `E(...)` produces the same unevaluated object as calling `Expectation(...)` directly, so either spelling works before `.expand()`.

Both approaches do real work up front, just different kinds. `reversed(text)` is an O(1) lazy iterator, but each `next()` goes through the generic reverse-iterator protocol (bounds check, index decrement, fetch as separate steps) — a small fixed per-element cost repeated n times. `text[::-1]` does an O(n) copy immediately, but as one tight C loop over contiguous memory, after which iteration is fast and direct. For short strings, the reversed-iterator's per-call overhead is negligible next to the interpreter/loop overhead in `count()`, so count1 wins by avoiding the allocation. As length grows, the slice-copy cost stays cheap per byte in C, while the accumulated per-element overhead of the generic `reversed` iterator (paid n times) grows to exceed it — so count2 catches up and overtakes. It's a classic fixed-cost-vs-per-element-cost crossover; the exact crossover point (~12-14 here) is implementation- and hardware-specific, not guaranteed by the language.

Missing: your Python/pdb version. Stock `pdb`'s `where`/`bt` has no built-in option to window or limit the frame range (unlike gdb's `bt n`) — it always dumps the whole stack. The practical fix is switching to `pdbpp` (`pip install pdbpp`; it monkeypatches `pdb` so `python -m pdb` picks it up automatically), whose `where`/`w` command accepts a count argument and shows only frames around the current one, e.g. `w 5`. If you can't add a dependency: use `up`/`down` to move near the frame you care about, then `l`/`ll` to see source there instead of the full trace; or drop into `interact` from pdb and slice `traceback.extract_stack()` yourself; or temporarily set `sys.setrecursionlimit()` lower so the crash happens near the real bug and there are simply fewer frames to scroll through in the first place.

sqlite3 doesn't support the `%(name)s` (pyformat) placeholder style — that's a psycopg2/MySQLdb convention. Python's `sqlite3` module only accepts `?` (positional, qmark) or `:name` (named) placeholders. Since your rows are dicts, switch to `:name`, which matches dict keys directly:
```python
c.executemany(
    "INSERT INTO AAPL1M2021 (time,open,high,low,close,volume) "
    "VALUES (:t,:o,:h,:l,:c,:v)",
    data
)
conn.commit()
```
No key renaming needed since your dict already uses `t, o, h, l, c, v`. Also make sure to call `conn.commit()` afterward, or the inserted rows won't be persisted to the `.db` file even once the syntax error is gone.

The problem is the stray `remote_side="Forum.id"` on `Game.root_forum`. `remote_side` exists to disambiguate direction in *self-referential* relationships (correctly used on your `Forum.parent`/`children` pair) — it's not meaningful between two different tables. Declaring it there makes SQLAlchemy re-derive `Game.root_forum` as many-to-one, matching `Forum.game` (also many-to-one via `game_id`), hence 'both of the same direction'. Since `Forum.game_id`→`Game.id` and `Game.root_forum_id`→`Forum.id` are two independent FKs forming a genuine one-to-one, just drop `remote_side`:
```python
root_forum: Mapped["Forum"] = relationship(
    "Forum", back_populates="game",
    primaryjoin="Game.root_forum_id == Forum.id",
    foreign_keys=[root_forum_id],
    uselist=False,
)
```
Keep `foreign_keys`/`primaryjoin`/`post_update=True` on the Forum side as-is — those correctly resolve the two-FK cycle; `remote_side` was the only piece causing the conflict.

Look closely at that character — it isn't an ASCII colon `:` (U+003A), it's `׃` (Hebrew Sof Pasuq, U+05C3), which merely looks like a colon in most fonts. Your `chars` list has the ASCII `":"`, so `.replace(":", "-")` never matches it, which is why only `|` got replaced. This isn't a loop bug — `str.replace` already replaces every occurrence in one call, no count limit needed. Fix by targeting the actual character, e.g. with a regex that also covers look-alikes by codepoint:
```python
import re
titre = re.sub(r'[?:*~|#/"\u05C3]', '-', titre)
```
Or copy the exact glyph from your source string into `chars` instead of typing an ASCII colon. For robustness against similar look-alike punctuation generally, you'd need a broader Unicode-category or confusable-character normalization pass, not just an extra literal in the list.

`dict(zip(results))` fails because `zip()` needs two separate iterables (keys, values); you passed it one list of row-tuples, and `dict()` can't turn raw rows into key/value pairs on its own. Column names come from `cursor.description`, not from `results`. Get them per table, zip each row against them, and nest under the table name:
```python
output = {}
for table in tables:
    cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM {table}")
    cols = [d[0] for d in cursor.description]
    rows = cursor.fetchall()
    output[table] = [dict(zip(cols, row)) for row in rows]
print(output)
```
This gives one dict per table, each a list of row-dicts keyed by column name. If you actually want one flat merged dict across all three tables, you need a unique key first (e.g. a primary key column), since a plain dict can't hold duplicate keys from different tables.

The label sits at the bottom initially because `self.updateLabel(0)` runs inside `__init__`, before the widget is shown or laid out — at that point `self.label.height()` and `self.slider.height()` are still default/zero, so `sliderPositionFromValue` computes a bogus `height`. It only looks right after resizing because `resizeEvent` fires once real geometry exists. Don't call `updateLabel` synchronously in `__init__`; defer it until Qt has real sizes:
```python
from PyQt5 import QtCore
...
QtCore.QTimer.singleShot(0, lambda: self.updateLabel(0))
```
or move the initial call into a `showEvent` override:
```python
def showEvent(self, ev):
    super().showEvent(ev)
    self.updateLabel(self.slider.value())
```
Either defers the position calculation until after the widget's actual layout is computed, matching what already happens correctly on later `resizeEvent` calls.

Your `again()` recurses instead of looping, and `while a and b >= 1` only checks truthiness of `a` and compares just `b`, not both — plus mixing recursive calls with `break` inside a nested loop makes the flow hard to reason about. Use one straightforward accumulation loop, no recursion:
```python
total = 0
while True:
    n = int(input("Enter a positive number (0 or negative to stop): "))
    if n <= 0:
        break
    total += n
print("Result", total)
```
This reads one number per prompt, stops the moment a value is ≤ 0, and prints the running total — matching 'adds an unspecified amount of positive numbers, stops on zero or negative.' If you need two numbers per round like your original (a, b), just add both to `total` before the next prompt, checking each against the stop condition before adding it.

What you're describing isn't mutating one list while iterating it — it's producing a new list at each step by dropping the original's last element and inserting `current_element` at position i, shifting the rest right:
```python
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3]
current_element = 99
for i in range(len(nums)):
    row = nums.copy()
    row.pop()                 # drop the last original element
    row.insert(i, current_element)
    print(row)
```
This prints `[99,0,1,2]`, `[0,99,1,2]`, `[0,1,99,2]`, `[0,1,2,99]` — exactly your example. If you instead want to genuinely mutate `nums` in place while looping safely, iterate `for i in range(len(nums)):` (indices, not the list itself) since iterating directly over a list you're inserting into causes elements to be skipped or repeated as positions shift under the iterator.

Manhattan distance gives a diamond (rotated square) because it measures |dx|+|dy|=r instead of true Euclidean distance. For a real 1-pixel-thick circle outline at an integer center/radius, use the midpoint (Bresenham) circle algorithm, computing one octant and mirroring it 8-way:
```python
def circle_border(cx, cy, r):
    points = set()
    x, y, d = r, 0, 1 - r
    while x >= y:
        for dx, dy in [(x,y),(y,x),(-x,y),(-y,x),
                       (x,-y),(y,-x),(-x,-y),(-y,-x)]:
            points.add((cx+dx, cy+dy))
        y += 1
        if d < 0:
            d += 2*y + 1
        else:
            x -= 1
            d += 2*(y-x) + 1
    return points
```
This gives exact integer pixel coordinates on the circle's edge with no gaps or duplicated diagonal artifacts, unlike a naive `round(r*cos), round(r*sin)` angle sweep.

You're fetching the GitHub *web page* that displays the file (`.../blob/master/...`), which returns HTML, not raw JSON — `json.loads` fails at line 8 because it's parsing markup, not data. Use the raw-content URL instead:
```python
import json, urllib.request
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ovi/DummyJSON/master/src/data/carts.json"
with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as resp:
    data = json.loads(resp.read().decode())
print(data)
```
Swap `github.com/<user>/<repo>/blob/<branch>/<path>` for `raw.githubusercontent.com/<user>/<repo>/<branch>/<path>` (drop `blob/`) whenever you want a file's actual contents rather than GitHub's rendered page. Your commented-out second attempt has the same problem plus another: it's a `tree/` directory-listing URL (also HTML), and `open()` expects a local filesystem path — it can't open an HTTP URL at all, so that would fail differently.

'self-signed certificate in certificate chain' means something between you and the server is terminating/re-signing TLS with a certificate not in Python's trusted store (`certifi`) — almost always a corporate proxy, firewall, or antivirus doing HTTPS inspection, not an actual defect in ConnectWise's own certificate. Don't set `verify=False`; instead trust that specific intercepting root CA. Export it (from your browser's trusted-root list, or ask IT) as a `.pem`, then either point requests at it:
```python
requests.get(url, verify="path/to/corporate_root.pem")
```
or append it to your certifi bundle so all libraries pick it up:
```python
import certifi
with open(certifi.where(), "ab") as f:
    f.write(open("corporate_root.pem", "rb").read())
```
or set the `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`/`SSL_CERT_FILE` environment variable to that combined path. On a home network with no proxy, this is more often antivirus HTTPS-scanning injecting its own root cert — check and whitelist that instead.
